title: Episode 173: Herbert Hoover: Black Tuesday, the Great Depression, and the Bonus Army (1929–1933)
description:
On October 29, 1929, just seven months into Herbert Hoover's presidency, the New York Stock Exchange collapsed in an unprecedented frenzy of panic selling known as Black Tuesday, wiping out thirty billion dollars in wealth and plunging the nation into the Great Depression. As five thousand banks failed, factory gates slammed shut, and unemployment soared to twenty-five percent, millions of destitute Americans congregated in cardboard shantytowns bitterly christened 'Hoovervilles.' Hoover worked eighteen-hour days, creating the landmark Reconstruction Finance Corporation and public works like the Hoover Dam, but his unbending philosophical refusal to provide direct federal cash relief turned public adoration into searing hatred. The tragedy culminated in the summer of 1932, when twenty thousand desperate World War I veterans of the Bonus Army marched on Washington, only to be routed with tanks, bayonets, and tear gas by General Douglas MacArthur. Discover the tragic fall of Herbert Hoover.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Today, we confront the agonizing downfall of Herbert Hoover. No president in American history experienced a more sudden and catastrophic reversal of fortune. From the summit of international veneration, Hoover was cast into the depths of public demonization as the Great Depression tore through the fabric of American society. Here is George with the story of Black Tuesday, the agony of the shantytowns, and the heartbreaking battle of Anacostia Flats.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: BLACK TUESDAY AND THE FINANCIAL DELUGE
Throughout the late 1920s, a speculative fever had seized the American imagination. Millions of ordinary citizens, captivated by newspaper headlines of overnight stock market fortunes, borrowed heavily on margin—putting down as little as ten percent cash to purchase wildly overvalued corporate shares. Hoover, privately terrified by the rampant speculation, had repeatedly warned Federal Reserve governors and Wall Street bankers that a catastrophic reckoning was imminent, but his warnings were brushed aside. On Thursday, October 24, 1929, the bubble burst. Stock prices tumbled into a bottomless pit as frantic margin calls triggered waves of automated liquidation. Five days later, on Black Tuesday, October 29, the market shattered entirely. A record sixteen million four hundred thousand shares changed hands in a hurricane of blind terror; tickers ran hours behind, fortunes evaporated in minutes, and the financial wealth of the United States contracted by thirty billion dollars—more than the entire cost of America's involvement in the First World War. What many believed was a temporary market adjustment soon revealed itself as the opening shockwave of a global economic Behind the ticker-tape ticker screens lay structural vulnerabilities: an agricultural sector already depressed for a decade, overleveraged banking institutions, and an unequal distribution of purchasing power that left consumer demand unable to absorb industrial output. The sudden evaporation of thirty billion dollars in wealth shattered the national illusion that paper speculation could substitute for sound economic production.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: THE SPIRAL INTO THE GREAT DEPRESSION
The Wall Street collapse quickly infected every artery of the American economy. Overextended banks that had invested depositors' funds in stocks or held uncollectible real estate loans began to crumble. Panicked crowds formed lines around city blocks to withdraw their life savings, triggering a cascading chain reaction of bank runs that shuttered more than five thousand financial institutions and erased the life savings of nine million families. As purchasing power vanished, factories slashed production, payrolls were slashed, and by 1932, one out of every four American workers—nearly thirteen million people—was completely unemployed. Across the nation, evicted families erected miserable shantytowns of rusted tin, cardboard crates, and packing boxes on the fringes of major cities, bitterly naming them 'Hoovervilles.' The newspapers that destitute men wrapped around their bodies to ward off freezing winds were called 'Hoover blankets'; empty pockets turned inside out were 'Hoover flags'; jackrabbits shot for meat in the dust-choked plains were 'Hoover hogs.' The man who had fed twenty million starving souls across Europe was now accused by his own countrymen of The contrast between his global reputation as the great humanitarian who fed Europe and his apparent paralysis in feeding starving Americans created a profound sense of popular betrayal and bitter cynicism. The human suffering of the depression cut Hoover to the quick, though his reserved Quaker nature prevented him from displaying his grief publicly.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: HOOVER'S INTERVENTIONS AND PHILOSOPHIC LIMITS
In historical fact, Herbert Hoover worked himself to the point of physical exhaustion, laboring eighteen hours a day in the Oval Office to halt the economic catastrophe. Defying the orthodox laissez-faire economic advice of Treasury Secretary Andrew Mellon—who famously advocated letting the crash 'liquidate labor, liquidate stocks, liquidate farmers, liquidate real estate'—Hoover initiated the most interventionist federal policies in peacetime history up to that date. He summoned railroad executives, industrial tycoons, and labor leaders to the White House, securing pledges to maintain wage rates and continue capital spending. He poured millions into public works projects, speeding construction on bridges, post offices, and the colossal Boulder Dam. In early 1932, he created the Reconstruction Finance Corporation—the RFC—a massive two-billion-dollar federal lending agency designed to bail out banks, railroads, and insurance companies to restore liquidity. Yet Hoover harbored a profound, unyielding philosophical boundary: he adamantly refused to approve direct, federal cash handouts to individual citizens. Believing that a federal dole would destroy the precious American character of self-reliance, local charity, and 'rugged individualism,' Hoover insisted that relief must remain the sacred duty of city governments, private philanthropies, and state authorities—Hoover could not bring himself to abandon his lifelong conviction that character was forged through self-reliance, failing to recognize that the scale of industrial unemployment had overwhelmed the capacity of private charity. His tragic refusal to approve direct federal cash relief stemmed from a deep philosophical fear of creating an all-powerful, coercive state.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE HAWLEY-SMOOT BLUNDER AND GLOBAL COLLAPSE
In June 1930, Hoover made what historians widely consider the most disastrous economic blunder of his presidency: signing the Hawley-Smoot Tariff Act. Passed by Congress in a misguided attempt to protect struggling American farmers from foreign competition, the act raised United States tariffs on more than twenty thousand imported goods to record, prohibitive levels. Over one thousand distinguished economists signed a joint petition begging Hoover to veto the bill, warning that it would provoke severe international retaliation and strangle world trade. Hoover, desperate to satisfy congressional Republicans, reluctantly signed the measure. The backlash was swift and devastating. Twenty-five foreign trading partners immediately enacted retaliatory tariffs against American exports, causing world trade to plunge by an astounding sixty-six percent between 1929 and 1934. When Austria's largest bank, the Creditanstalt, collapsed in May 1931, the European financial system imploded, forcing Great Britain off the gold standard and triggering a fresh wave of panic and bank failures across the United States. Hoover's brilliant attempt to stabilize the international financial order by declaring a one-year moratorium on World War I intergovernmental debts provided only temporary respite against the By attempting to protect domestic production through punitive trade barriers, the administration accelerated the breakdown of international commerce and deepened the misery of farmers and factory workers alike. The collapse of international trade following the tariff war demonstrated the intricate interdependence of the modern global economy.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE BONUS EXPEDITIONARY FORCE OF 1932
The defining human drama of Hoover's presidency erupted in the sweltering summer of 1932 with the arrival of the Bonus Army. In 1924, Congress had enacted the World War Adjusted Compensation Act, granting World War I veterans certificates payable with interest in 1945—a future bonus for their wartime sacrifice. But as destitution and hunger swept the land, twenty thousand impoverished veterans, led by an unemployed former soldier named Walter W. Waters, formed the 'Bonus Expeditionary Force.' Hitchhiking and hopping freight trains from Oregon, Pennsylvania, and across the nation, the veterans converged on Washington with their wives and children, demanding the immediate cash payment of their bonus certificates. Camping peaceably on the mudflats of Anacostia across the river from the Capitol, the veterans built a disciplined, orderly shantytown with military hygiene, daily bugle calls, and parades down Pennsylvania Avenue. When the Senate voted down the Bonus Bill on June 17, thousands of veterans assembled outside the Capitol groaned in bitter disappointment, yet sang 'America' and marched quietly back to their camp. Hoover generously provided surplus army tents, field kitchens, and medical aid, but as the hot summer dragged on, government officials became gripped by the irrational fear that the camp was secretly Despite official paranoia, the vast majority of veterans were patriotic family men who carried American flags, saluted the colors, and asked only for the financial relief that Congress had promised them. The Bonus Army marchers represented the heart and soul of the nation's working class, veterans whose sacrifice deserved honor and dignity.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: THE BATTLE OF ANACOSTIA FLATS
On July 28, 1932, the tragedy reached its horrifying climax. When local police attempted to clear several abandoned treasury buildings on Pennsylvania Avenue occupied by veterans, a melee broke out. Rocks were hurled, police opened fire, and two unarmed veterans, William Hushka and Eric Carlson, were fatally shot. A shaken District of Columbia commission informed Hoover that civil order had collapsed. Hoover ordered the Secretary of War to clear the downtown government buildings, strictly instructing that the troops should not cross the bridge into the main Anacostia refugee camp. But the operation was placed under the command of General Douglas MacArthur, the theatrical, authoritarian Army Chief of Staff. Accompanied by his young aides, Major Dwight D. Eisenhower and Major George S. Patton, MacArthur dressed in full dress uniform and rode a white horse, accompanied by six light tanks, five hundred infantrymen with fixed bayonets, and cavalry with sabers drawn. Sweeping through downtown Washington, the soldiers fired clouds of tear gas into the crowds of onlookers. Then, in flagrant, deliberate violation of President Hoover's explicit written orders, MacArthur crossed the 11th Street Bridge into Anacostia Flats. Troopers hurled tear-gas canisters into tents and torched the wooden shanties. As night fell, flames lit up the Washington sky; hundreds of veterans and their families fled in terror, clutching their crying children. Hoover, horrified by MacArthur's insubordination, loyally refused to publicly repudiate his general, bearing the full moral blame for the assault upon America's own wounded war heroes. The violent assault on Anacostia Flats shocked the conscience of the nation and permanently stained the reputation of the administration.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE VERDICT OF 1932 AND THE LONG TWILIGHT
The images of American soldiers gassing World War I veterans and burning their shelters sealed Herbert Hoover's political doom. In Albany, New York, Democratic presidential nominee Franklin D. Roosevelt read the morning newspapers, looked up at his advisor Felix Frankfurter, and said quietly: 'There is nothing inside the man. This means I will win the election.' In the autumn campaign of 1932, Hoover traveled by train across a hostile, jeering country, his speeches interrupted by boos and rotting vegetables hurled at his train windows. Roosevelt crushed Hoover in an electoral landslide of four hundred and seventy-two to fifty-nine. Hoover left the White House a deeply bitter, misunderstood man, mourning the collapse of the prosperity he had dreamed of securing. Yet in the decades following World War II, Hoover achieved a historic personal renaissance. President Harry S. Truman summoned the elder statesman out of retirement in 1946 to coordinate post-war famine relief for starving Europeans, where Hoover once again saved millions of lives. He later chaired the celebrated Hoover Commissions, reorganizing and modernizing the executive branch of government. By the time he passed away in 1964 at the age of ninety, Herbert Hoover's legacy had come full circle: a tragic president, but an undisputed, immortal giant of humanitarian grace. Hoover's later resurgence as a revered elder statesman proved that character and dedication to service outlast the fleeting verdicts of political defeat.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
The tragedy of Herbert Hoover proved that even the most brilliant administrative intellect and humanitarian dedication cannot overcome rigid ideological dogma in the face of an existential economic catastrophe. From the ashes of Hoover's defeat emerged the most transformative president of the twentieth century. Next week, we begin our exploration of Franklin Delano Roosevelt: his heroic battle against polio, his electrifying proclamation that 'the only thing we have to fear is fear itself,' the whirlwind miracle of the First Hundred Days, and the birth of the New Deal. Until then, thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories.
